Consistency.justification: The proposal is strongly aligned with the stated idea of single-shot hyperspectral wavefront sensing using a multicore fiber, angular memory effects, spectral decorrelation, speckle encoding, and Hartmann-like gradient measurements. Its objectives, forward model, metrics, and baselines directly address the spatial-spectral trade-off highlighted in the idea. The learned mask and physics-informed reconstruction are coherent extensions of the cited demonstration. Minor inconsistencies remain: the hypothesis mentions optimizing properties such as per-core length, whereas the experimental parameterization mainly specifies core position, effective NA, and an overall scale; moreover, the claimed optimization of a fabricated mask is not fully matched by the proposed bench experiment using a commercial bundle and unspecified simple modifications. The literature discussion is relevant but too abbreviated to establish that the proposed combination has not already been explored in related learned-optics or transmission-matrix work.

Clarity.justification: The proposal has a clear motivation, hypothesis, experimental workflow, set of baselines, evaluation metrics, ablations, and risk analysis. The division into forward modeling, mask optimization, inversion, calibration, and validation makes the research plan easy to follow. However, several central details remain underspecified. The exact camera-image formation equation, representation of the hyperspectral wavefront cube, wavelength discretization, treatment of phase ambiguities, and coupling between spot displacement and wavelength-dependent speckle are not precisely defined. It is also unclear whether mutual information will actually be estimated or merely approximated through reconstruction loss, and what constitutes a realizable per-core modification in the physical experiment.

Novelty.justification: Jointly optimizing a multicore Hartmann mask and a physics-informed neural inversion for hyperspectral wavefront recovery is a reasonably original and potentially valuable combination. In particular, optimizing geometry for both spatial-gradient localization and spectral discriminability, rather than applying learning only to reconstruction, could produce useful new design principles. Nevertheless, the main methodological ingredients—differentiable optical design, learned reconstruction, data-fidelity losses, spectral priors, and calibration-based speckle inversion—are established in computational imaging. The novelty therefore lies primarily in their application and integration in this specific multicore-fiber sensing architecture. A more systematic comparison with learned coded apertures, transmission-matrix inversion, fiber-based computational imaging, and task-specific optical co-design is needed to substantiate stronger novelty claims.

Soundness.justification: The proposal rests on plausible physical mechanisms and includes several sound practices: measured spectral calibration, differentiable data fidelity, manufacturability constraints, fixed-mask controls, classical baselines, ablations, robustness tests, and evaluation on simulated and real targets. However, the forward model appears substantially simplified relative to the actual coherent propagation problem. Parameterizing spectral behavior mainly through a correlation function may not preserve the phase-sensitive, wavelength-dependent transmission response needed to render raw speckle images accurately. A correlation width alone generally does not specify individual speckle realizations or their response to changing local incidence angle. Identifiability is also insufficiently analyzed: recovering a phase map at many wavelengths from one intensity image can be highly underdetermined, and smoothness, low-rank, or sparse priors may drive apparent performance without guaranteeing faithful recovery. The proposal lacks information-theoretic bounds, uncertainty estimates, explicit handling of phase gauge and unwrapping, and a rigorous protocol for preventing inverse crime in simulation. The use of different spectral priors, including smooth spectra and line spectra, is sensible but may require different models or objectives rather than one universally effective regularizer.

Feasibility.justification: A simulation study and a learned inversion for a fixed commercial multicore bundle are feasible with current optical hardware and machine-learning tools. Tunable-source calibration, SLM-generated wavefronts, synthetic augmentation, and GPU inference are realistic in a well-equipped laboratory. The less feasible component is experimental validation of the optimized hardware. Arbitrary core positions and per-core NA values are not readily adjustable in an existing commercial bundle, while custom multicore-fiber fabrication can be expensive and slow. The phrase simple fiber modifications does not explain how optimized internal core geometry or per-core optical properties would be implemented. Calibration dimensionality may also be much larger than suggested because the response can depend jointly on wavelength, input angle, polarization, temperature, bending, and core coupling. These issues do not preclude the project, but they may restrict it to simulated mask optimization plus experimental validation of reconstruction on a fixed mask unless fabrication access and stability controls are specified.

Significance.justification: Compact single-shot measurement of wavelength-resolved wavefronts is relevant to optical metrology, adaptive optics, ultrafast or dispersive imaging, and systems in which scanning is undesirable. Demonstrating a better spatial-spectral trade-off and robust reconstruction from a compact optical head would be a meaningful contribution. The planned ablations and design recommendations could also be useful beyond one device. The likely impact is moderated by strong prior dependence, calibration burden, environmental sensitivity of fiber speckle, and fundamental limits imposed by detector sampling, photon budget, and spectral correlation width. The proposal does not yet quantify the target improvement, operating bandwidth, wavelength resolution, field of view, or comparison against alternative hyperspectral wavefront sensors, so transformative impact is not established.

strengths: Strong alignment with the target sensing concept and a coherent end-to-end plan combining optical design, physical constraints, calibration, baselines, ablations, and real-data validation.
Addresses an important spatial-spectral trade-off and could yield useful reconstruction improvements and practical multicore-mask design guidance.
weaknesses: The proposed forward model and identifiability analysis are not rigorous enough for the highly underdetermined, coherent, wavelength-dependent inverse problem; spectral correlation functions alone may be inadequate for raw-image prediction.

The physical experiment does not clearly validate the optimized hardware because commercial bundles cannot readily realize arbitrary optimized core layouts or per-core properties, and the required modifications and calibration burden are insufficiently specified.
